The graph above shows $y=k{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+c.$ Find the value of $k-c.$
worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=\frac{4}{3},$ hence $c=\frac{4}{3}.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,2),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=2$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+\frac{4}{3} & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{4})}^{0}+\frac{4}{3} & =2 \\ k+\frac{4}{3} & =2 \\ k & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
k-c=\frac{2}{3}-\frac{4}{3}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=\frac{2}{3}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+\frac{4}{3}.$
